newsitem.title: INDIA: India seen passing budget even without Chidambaram.
newsitem.headline: India seen passing budget even without Chidambaram.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's angry departure from the government has raised a cloud over the fate of his market-friendly budget, but analysts said on Sunday it would clear parliament even without him.

"By and large, the Finance Bill as proposed by Chidambaram will go through parliament, perhaps with some minor amendments, and we can celebrate the depoliticisation of the budget," said Charan Wadhva of New Delhi's Centre for Policy Research.

Parliament was due to meet in a special session starting on Monday to consider the 1997/98 (April-March) budget, containing a battery of tax-cutting and tariff-reduction proposals that Chidambaram presented in February and which delighted markets.
Chidambaram on Sunday refused to discuss the budget.
Asked to comment on its fate, he told Reuters: "I'm not going to talk about it. You should ask the new government."
Economic analysts said prime minister-in-waiting Inder Kumar Gujral would need to appoint a new finance minister to pilot the budget proposals through parliament.
"A new finance minister would have every right to change it, but they would be only minor amendments, not drastic changes," Wadhva told Reuters.
With the support of 140 votes from its ally, the Congress party, the United Front's 178 lawmakers should easily push the budget through the 542-member lower house of parliament.
Economist Sanjaya Baru said Gujral might curtail a proposed reduction in taxes on business and higher income groups to appease communist members of the coalition who backed his appointment.

Chidambaram's Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) announced on Saturday it would pull out of the government but continue to support the United Front alliance in parliament, minutes after Gujral was nominated as the coalition's new leader.
The United Front has staked a claim to form a new centre-left government after electing Gujral to succeed caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.

TMC leader G.K. Moopanar had been considered a favourite for the job, and the powerful regional group's decision to withdraw could merely be a tactic to press Gujral into luring party representatives back with cabinet posts, analysts said.
They said Chidambaram, one of the architects of India's economic liberalisation programme, might even be persuaded to return to its fold.
"I would think Gujral would try and persuade the TMC, and if he fails, he will have to look for someone who will sell with the market. Chidambaram would be happy to return," Baru said.
If Chidambaram remained adamant, Gujral could turn to outgoing Industry Minister Murasoli Maran, an economic liberal, as a successor sure to please markets, Baru said.
"On the other hand, he could bring in someone from outside (the coalition). It would really be a coup if he could persuade Manmohan Singh to return," he said.

Singh, a Congress deputy, was the finance minister who initiated India's pathbreaking economic reforms programme in 1991 and steered the country through five years of free trade policies as it shrugged off decades of socialist controls.
Congress has not ruled out joining the new alliance.
